positions.detail: patrickhlauke opened #190 arguing that although SVG contains real text elements and so passes the normative definition of images of text, no user agent lets a user change the font, size or colour of that text, which is the whole point of the criterion. alastc agrees the intent is not met and proposes a split: if the text's size, position and colour must be relative to its surroundings, as in a graph or infographic, it meets the "particular visual effect" carve-out; otherwise it fails. He puts the colour half at user agents and treats the font and spacing half as inherent to SVG's purpose.

positions.label: SVG can be made to comply if authored carefully
positions.detail: Walks the criterion property by property and finds browser zoom, font size, font family, letter spacing and word spacing all work in SVG, with line-height and paragraph spacing the only genuine gaps. Argues those were not required until WCAG 2.1's 1.4.12, which only forbids preventing adaptation rather than requiring the author to offer it, so SVG text should not be held to a higher bar. Later narrows this after testing goodwitch's examples: he would only pass an SVG that inherits the document's colours, because adjusting fill values per graphic demands CSS expertise and time most users do not have.

positions.label: A sad low pass, and the group should rule
positions.detail: Built three CodePen examples and concluded that SVG with text passes, SVG with path-drawn text fails, and an svg file loaded via img fails. Pushes back on JAWS-test that High Contrast Mode is not named in the normative text and the criterion nowhere says customisation must be easy, so on a strict normative reading this has to pass. Asks AGWG to make a ruling so the industry is consistent, and suggests the real fix belongs in a WCAG 2.x release or Silver.

positions.label: Move detectable text under text-to-speech
positions.detail: Reports in #202 that the text-to-speech subgroup could find nothing specific to text-to-speech devices that a screen reader would not also cover, and proposes moving Detectable text out of Clear meaning into the Text-to-speech section to replace the Text-to-speech supported requirement. Also asks whether "text-to-speech" names the technology or the capability, suggesting a rename such as "Text as speech" if the latter, and where user-agent and TTS developer guidance would live in WCAG 3. No one has replied.

positions.label: Programmatic determinability is not enough
positions.detail: In #537, calls the provision a step in the right direction that stops short: text that is programmatically determinable but cannot be selected breaks select-to-speak. Also flags possible redundancy with the copying-supported part of "Avoid exclusionary cognitive tasks" and suggests the two may be better combined or regrouped. Unanswered.

agreed: Line-height and paragraph spacing are the properties SVG genuinely cannot expose to CSS adjustment; JAWS-test's inventory of the rest was not contested.
Text drawn as SVG paths rather than text elements fails, which nobody disputed.
open: Whether SVG text passes on a strict normative reading or fails on intent. goodwitch asked AGWG for a ruling in 2020 and none is recorded in the thread.
Whether High Contrast Mode counts as a form of setting colour and background — JAWS-test raised it and expected most of the group to say no.
shawnthompson's proposal in #202 to relocate Detectable text under Text-to-speech, and the naming question behind it.
sydneycolemanfromgoogle's point in #537 that selectability, not just programmatic determinability, is what select-to-speak needs.
text-detectable.note: Issue #190 is a WCAG 2.x-era discussion from 2019-2020 that has drawn no comment since, now carried forward under this provision's label. The two WCAG 3-era issues, #202 and #537, are both single unanswered comments.

disabled-controls-explained.headline: Light discussion across two issues: a 2019-2020 exchange over whether disabled controls need a mandated icon or just adequate contrast, and a separate COGA request that explanations be persistent rather than transient.

positions.label: Require a disabled icon or 3:1 contrast
positions.detail: DavidMacDonald opened #197 noting that disabled interface elements work badly for people with low vision precisely because WCAG 2 exempts them from 1.4.3, and proposed requiring either 3:1 contrast or an icon marking the element as disabled. bkimmel seconds the problem, particularly where disabled states are used to signal future potential — fill these in and you can submit — calling the exemption a large safe harbour that cuts against the Perceivable goal. bkimmel is explicitly unsure an icon is the right remedy.

positions.label: Contrast yes, mandated icons no
positions.detail: Would rather see some minimum contrast applied to solve readability than have WCAG start demanding icons everywhere, which impinges on visual design decisions. Suggests a more general intent of "indicating that something is disabled" as the flexible form. Also notes a likely crossover with how user agents themselves indicate disabled state.

positions.label: The definitions do not cover disabled elements
positions.detail: Points out that "Interactive elements distinguishable" is adjacent to this problem, but the definition of interactive element — responds to user input and has a distinct programmatically determinable name — excludes disabled elements, which instead fall under non-interactive element. Since disabled elements are not mentioned in the examples or notes around that definition, he questions what the group actually intends, and floats broadening the term or adding a new one for elements that exist to be interactive but may conditionally be disabled or read-only. Flags this provision as also applicable and links w3c/wcag#5053.

positions.label: Explanations must persist long enough to read
positions.detail: Filing for the COGA Task Force in #783, notes the provision requires that information explaining why a control is disabled be available but says nothing about timing or persistence. A snackbar that vanishes after three seconds fails a user with slower processing speed. Recommends requiring explanations be persistent and visually co-located, and asks that this be checked for compatibility with "Notifications adjustable" in the User Control section. Cites MCU 3.1.2, 3.2.1, 3.7.5 and A.4.

agreed: Disabled controls being exempt from contrast requirements is a real low-vision problem worth addressing — nobody in #197 disputed the premise, only the remedy.
alastc took #197 off the WCAG 2.2 slate in 2020 as needing more work, consideration and research, and it has stayed there.
open: Whether the fix is contrast, an icon, or a technology-neutral requirement to indicate disabled state — patrickhlauke's objection to mandating icons has gone unanswered since 2020.
Whether the definitions of interactive and non-interactive element should be revised to account for disabled and read-only states, raised by adampage.
julierawe's persistence and co-location requirement, filed in August 2026 with no replies.
disabled-controls-explained.note: #197 predates WCAG 3 and sat untouched from 2020 until adampage revived it in May 2026. #783 has drawn no response at all.

interactive-elements-distinguishable.headline: No discussion of this provision on its own terms — the single labelled thread is a 2019 issue about disabled controls, which reaches this provision only through adampage's closing comment that the definition of interactive element excludes disabled elements.

positions.label: The definition of interactive element leaves disabled controls out
positions.detail: The provision requires interactive elements to be visually distinguishable from static content without interaction and to include visual cues on how to use them, but the defined term covers only elements that respond to user input and have a distinct programmatically determinable name. Disabled elements therefore fall outside it and instead match non-interactive element, an element that does not respond to user input and does not include sub-parts. Because disabled elements are not named in the example or notes around that definition, adampage asks what the group intends and suggests broadening the term, or adding a new one, for elements that exist to be interactive but may conditionally be disabled or read-only. Links w3c/wcag#5053 as related.

positions.label: Underlying ask in #197: mark disabled controls perceivably
positions.detail: DavidMacDonald opened #197 in 2019 proposing that disabled UI elements meet 3:1 contrast or carry a disabled icon, since WCAG 2 exempts them from 1.4.3 and that hurts low-vision users. bkimmel seconded the problem — disabled states used to advertise future interaction create a large safe harbour — while doubting an icon is the answer. patrickhlauke preferred a minimum contrast plus a general intent of indicating disabled state, arguing WCAG cannot start demanding icons everywhere, and noted a possible crossover with user agents' own disabled styling.

agreed: Nothing about this provision's own wording has been settled here; the only substantive claim on record, adampage's reading of the two definitions, is unrebutted.
open: Whether the definition of interactive element should be broadened, or a new term introduced, to cover conditionally disabled and read-only controls — adampage's question, unanswered since May 2026.
alastc took #197 off the WCAG 2.2 slate in 2020 as needing more research, and it has not been picked back up in substance.
interactive-elements-distinguishable.note: This provision is exploratory and shares its only thread with "Disabled controls explained" and "Interactive element contrast sufficient"; it has attracted no issue of its own.

page-view-audio-adjustable.headline: A short 2020 exchange about why WCAG 2 allows autoplaying audio 3 seconds but auto-updating content 5, ending with agreement not to touch it in the 2.x series and an unpursued suggestion that WCAG 3 regroup audio with motion.

positions.label: Harmonise the limits and regroup the requirement
positions.detail: Opened #181 arguing the 3-versus-5-second split is hard to measure and has no rationale: a screen reader user is not less patient than a sighted one, and the two-second gap just adds complexity for testers. Also questions why autoplaying audio sits under Perceivable while auto-updating content sits under Operable, when unstoppable loud audio blocks operation exactly as animation does. Proposes raising 1.4.2 from 3 seconds to 5 for backwards compatibility, and treating WCAG 3 as the opportunity to group all page-level sound and animation together.

positions.label: Not worth a backwards-incompatible change
positions.detail: alastc notes the limits were set around 14 years earlier and no explanation is to hand, and that changing them would likely be backwards-incompatible — content passing WCAG 2.2 might not pass 2.0 or 2.1 — so he asks what the benefit would be. bruce-usab offers the historical guess that annoying sounds used to start immediately while animation and video took a few seconds to load, and five seconds of unwanted music was plainly too much. He does not claim the distinction is coherent, but would rather not make this change in the 2.x series.

agreed: The 3-versus-5-second difference has no principled justification anyone in the thread could produce.
Whatever the merits, it should not be changed within WCAG 2.x — bruce-usab's position, and consistent with alastc's backwards-compatibility concern.
open: Wildebrew's actual proposal — that WCAG 3 group autoplaying audio with page-level animation and auto-updating content rather than keeping them apart — was never answered and the thread stopped in April 2020.
page-view-audio-adjustable.note: Three comments total, all from 2020, in a thread carrying both this provision's label and "No visual motion". Wildebrew's second comment is a mail reply with the quoted email trailer left in.

no-nested-clauses.headline: Five mostly single-comment issues circling one question — whether a rule about clause nesting is feasible, useful and valid outside English — with only chaals and murata2makoto offering substantive argument and neither answered.

positions.label: Too hard for authors without writing resources
positions.detail: julierawe opened #552 carrying a January 2026 survey comment from sydneycolemanfromgoogle that the requirement will be incredibly challenging for parties without dedicated writing support and does not seem to add significantly to understanding. julierawe's answer is procedural and tooling-based: the requirement was moved from core to supplemental after the survey closed, which may resolve part of the concern, and free AI tools already flag complex sentence structures, so WCAG 3 could encourage them to call out nested clauses specifically.

positions.label: Not too hard, but too simplistic
positions.detail: Concedes the requirement takes real work and is very hard without someone who works on language, but notes few sites have nobody working on content, so difficulty is not the objection. Accepts that removing nested clauses generally does improve understanding, much more so for deep nesting. His actual complaint is that the requirement is too simple to be very useful: it does not differentiate by depth, clear writing is hard to test because people disagree on what is clear, and rules differ between languages so a test built for one is often useless in another.

positions.label: The premise is English-specific
positions.detail: Argues in #569 that clause nesting is not inherently a readability problem. The English centre-embedded example about the rat, the cat and the dog is genuinely hard to process, but the equivalent Japanese structure is unremarkable for native speakers, and the same holds for Korean and other head-final languages. Concludes that the real source of difficulty varies by language — word order ambiguity, unclear referents — and that treating nested clauses as a general problem overgeneralises from English.

positions.label: Editorial fixes to the examples
positions.detail: In #529 sydneycolemanfromgoogle asked whether "aced" should be replaced in a pass example as an idiom that may be hard to translate; hidde changed it to "did well on" in commit b1351ad and closed the issue on merge. In the still-open #530 sydneycolemanfromgoogle notes the listed nesting conjunctions may read as exhaustive when words like "that" also qualify, and supplies a rewritten test procedure making the list open-ended.

agreed: "Aced" was an inappropriate example word and has been replaced in the draft — the only thing actually resolved across these five issues.
Removing nested clauses generally does aid comprehension in English, which chaals grants even while objecting to the requirement's form.
open: Whether moving the requirement from core to supplemental addresses sydneycolemanfromgoogle's feasibility objection — julierawe proposed reaching out to ask and no outcome is recorded.
Whether it should move further, from supplemental to best practice, raised at the February 3rd AG meeting and tracked in #560 with no comments since.
Whether the requirement should account for nesting depth rather than treating any nesting alike (chaals).
Whether the requirement is valid for head-final languages at all (murata2makoto), unanswered since February 2026.
sydneycolemanfromgoogle's proposed non-exhaustive rewording of the conjunction list in #530.
no-nested-clauses.note: #560 summarises an AG meeting rather than hosting discussion: it records unnamed members raising feasibility concerns with specialized content, and another member citing complex sentence structures as a significant cognitive barrier in their own experience. Four of the five issues have zero or one comment.
